entry.title: Bill Hader’s Feature Directorial Debut ‘They Know’ Lands at Black Bear
entry.summary: Hader directs and stars alongside Linda Cardellini in the psychological horror film about co-parenting after a divorce.
entry.content:
Bill Hader‘s first film as a director has found its distribution partner. Black Bear has acquired North American distribution rights to “They Know,” Hader’s upcoming psychological horror film that he co-stars in with Linda Cardellini. The growing distributor, which just released “Wicker” nationwide, acquired the rights from financier MRC in what was described as a competitive situation.

Per an official synopsis, “They Know” follows a divorced dad who becomes increasingly suspicious and paranoid that his ex-wife’s new mysterious partner is exerting a strange, unsettling influence on their children.

“Bill Hader is a singular talent both in front of and behind the camera, and he has delivered a film in ‘They Know’ unlike anything we’ve ever seen,” Black Bear president of production & operations Michael Heimler said in a statement. “’They Know’ is authentic, original, and bold filmmaking at the highest level, and we couldn’t be more excited to partner with Bill and re-team with our great friends at MRC, who consistently deliver boundary-pushing films that help define their genre.”

Related Stories
Why Good Voice Acting Doesn’t Have to Happen in Isolation
Watch the ‘Backrooms’ VFX Supervisor Explain His Unique Process of Collaborating with Kane Parsons

Hader co-wrote “They Know” with Duffy Boudreau and produced alongside Bob Graf, with Alyssa Donovan co-producing.

Hader is a three-time Primetime Emmy winner for his work on “South Park” and “Barry.” He co-created the HBO comedy “Barry” with Alec Berg and began directing episodes in Season 2, gradually working his way up to directing the entirety of Season 4. He has long been open about his cinematic influences and his desire to transition into feature filmmaking after the show ended.

Hader recently shared some more details about directing his first feature while speaking at IndieWire’s Los Angeles Future of Filmmaking Summit. He explained that “They Know” emerged after he and longtime friend and writing partner Boudreau both went through divorces and discussed their biggest fears about ways the process could have gone awry.

“We’re both divorced. We were talking about how lucky we were that we were on, like, we had really good terms with our ex-wives, and we have kids with them,” Hader said. “We started talking about the worst case scenarios of, ‘Oh, my god, this person is going through this and this person is going through that.’ And then this idea came up.”

Black Bear has yet to announce a release date for “They Know.”

entry.title: Why Good Voice Acting Doesn’t Have to Happen in Isolation
entry.summary: "Wildwood" and "Tangles" Directors Travis Knight and Leah Nelson tell IndieWire about helping shape vocal performances for animation.
entry.content:
Film is always a collaborative medium, but one of the special things about animation is that you can craft incredibly nuanced performances with people who never get to meet. Voice acting in animation is a discipline in its own right — as legends like Mel Blanc and Eric Bauza show — where actors impart a kind of electric energy that carries through into the art style of what they’re voicing. So is voice directing. And the secret to both is in providing foundations for animators to build something bigger.

“Wildwood” director Travis Knight did a lot of the directing of his voice cast in lockdown Zooms, and hodge-podge recording setups, where it can be hard to remember that you’re developing something that needs to spiritually connect to the animation, whether existing animatics already exist or not. There isn’t the same kind of immersiveness for actors that live-action sets, costumes, and the basic pleasure of getting to read lines against other actors all provide. They have to build it from scratch.

Related Stories
Watch the ‘Backrooms’ VFX Supervisor Explain His Unique Process of Collaborating with Kane Parsons
Aaron Pierre on ‘Lanterns,’ the DC Shake-Up, and Landing a Role in Ryan Gosling’s ‘Star Wars’ Movie

“It asks something very different of an actor, which is challenging because an actor can bring so much to performance before they even utter a word,” Knight told IndieWire on an episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “So when you cast these things, it’s really interesting because sometimes the things we love about actors are not their voice; it’s everything else. So we will always listen, we’ll take clips from actors’ other films and their interviews, and we’ll put them against a design of a character.”

Hearing a voice against a design can be revelatory, Knight believes, because it can teach a director and an animation team about who a character really is, whether a performer is really going to work or not, even before they step into the booth. It’s also an important way to help sort the whole of an ensemble so that actors occupy different aural frequencies and accents, and don’t sound too similar. You want to really be able to feel the difference between Carey Mulligan’s powerfully sinister Alexandra and Angela Bassett’s regal General.

And then, once the voice cast is in the booth, it’s also on the director and the team to help each voice actor sketch out all the different permutations of emotion the animators will then use as inspiration, and as tools.

“You’ll get the scene 30, 40, 50 different ways,” Knight said. “It takes forever. But, in the end, if you can do it properly, it feels like these characters are living in the same scene at the same time. And then it comes down to the animator to try to figure out how they can match the beauty of the vocal performance with the physical performance.”

That’s the normal process for feature animation: finding compelling voices, matching them with a design that feels spiritually connected to that voice, covering the performance many different ways, and then assembling a template for animators to build off of. And it’s the director, really, who has to hold in their head the many ways that the disparate parts will all come together.

“An animator is an actor, but they’re just acting through their hands and through a puppet, and it’s two actors collaborating to create a complete performance. But oftentimes it happens across space, across time. And when it comes together in a harmonious way, it’s really beautiful because this thing seems like it’s completely alive,” Knight said.

But sometimes, voice actors’ performances do get to be alive together. That was a key creative choice that director Leah Nelson made for “Tangles” — it’s hard to argue with the logic of putting Abbi Jacobson, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, and Bryan Cranston all in a room together to act out an earnest family drama, even if there’s a bit of mic bleed.

“I’m so glad we [put them together]. And it wasn’t that hard. It took a little bit of scheduling Tetris to get it done, but it was so worthwhile,” Nelson told IndieWire. “Abbi does a ton of voice work, and often they’re alone and not even able to have someone to read against them. Sometimes they’re just doing the lines and sort of jumping around. And what I ultimately wanted was to have this really naturalistic dialogue.”

“Tangles” boasts naturalism when it comes to sound, from bespoke foley to overlapping banter that isn’t meant to be precisely understood but to convey the chaos of one’s own (infuriating, loving) family. So Nelson and her team embraced the ways actors can build on each other, and even on improv, in recording the dialogue.

“A lot of humor came out of giving them time to not only play with the dialogue but to play with each other. But also, those really intimate and difficult moments of the film, they could look in each other’s eyes and work through those moments. That was important to me, and it was important to them as well. So it was an experience we all went through together.”

The one downside of treating recording sessions more like the rehearsals for a play is the risk of wrecking takes. “We spent a lot of time at the table trying to hold [our reactions] in or like, ‘Don’t sneeze! Nobody move!’” Nelson joked. “But I didn’t want it to sound like there was so much suturing; the mastery of the dialogue editing to make it all sound naturalistic, so we also did a lot of work to make that happen. But what we had to work with felt very naturalistic to begin with.”

The ultimate example of naturalistic voice acting, however, might be on display in “Wildwood.” Knight’s own son was a newborn while the team was laying down track for the film, which made him the perfect actor for the role of kidnapped Baby Mac.

“I essentially chased him around the house with a digital recorder. Sometimes with my iPhone. I was just trying to coax things out of him, make him laugh and giggle and verbalize. And the thing about babies is that they’re constantly trying to make sense of the world,” Knight said. “They’re always babbling and trying to make shapes with their mouths. So we have a lot of that babbling in the movie, and it helped make it feel naturalistic.”

It speaks to the wide-ranging power of voice acting in animation: you can get to naturalism through a grounded collaboration between actors, an actor in complete isolation, or hitting “record” on an iPhone while you’re changing a diaper.

“Wildwood” is now in theaters. “Tangles” releases in theaters on January 15, 2027.

entry.title: Watch the ‘Backrooms’ VFX Supervisor Explain His Unique Process of Collaborating with Kane Parsons
entry.summary: Watch 'Backrooms' VFX supervisor Edward Douglas discuss working with Kane Parsons at IndieWire's Craft Roundtables.
entry.content:
When you hire a 20-year-old director to adapt his own viral YouTube series into a major Hollywood film, you’re not going to end up with a traditional movie. That’s part of what made Kane Parsons’ “Backrooms” such a massive critical and commercial success for A24. Audiences were eager to embrace Parsons as a major new filmmaking voice — and his crew members were just as excited for the chance to work with him.

During IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, “Backrooms” VFX Supervisor Edward Douglas broke down the unique workflow that he developed with Parsons during pre-production. He explained that Parsons was used to making his own effects in Blender, so the team started communicating with him using the popular VFX software.

Related Stories
Aaron Pierre on ‘Lanterns,’ the DC Shake-Up, and Landing a Role in Ryan Gosling’s ‘Star Wars’ Movie
Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a New Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’

“The first conversation I had with Kane Parsons was ‘How do you like to work?’ And we embraced his process,” Douglas said. “Because his way of communicating with the entire crew was first, through Blender. He built 100,000 square feet of sets in Blender and passed it off to the production designer. And it immediately crashed his computer. But that let us start breaking down everything.”

Despite costing less than $10 million, “Backrooms” contained a significant number of VFX shots. Douglas explained that the process became a unique mix of traditional effects work by seasoned pros and found-footage-style shots that Parsons did himself.

“It was an indie budget film, but it had over ten minutes of full CG,” Douglas said. “Some of it was traditional, and some of it was Backrooms found footage exploration. That ended up being a hybrid VFX process. We had very traditional sequences when we were working with VFX Blenders. And then we had more of our Kane Parsons DIY pipeline for scenes that he would really be touching himself. And we set it up so that Kane could actually log into the VFX Blender servers and tweak things, set up shots. Because that was his way. He could say, ‘Here are the notes,’ or Can I show you?’ And we’d want to create a way for him to show us. Because he is, at his heart, a VFX artist.”

More coverage from IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables will be published here over the coming weeks.

entry.title: Aaron Pierre on ‘Lanterns,’ the DC Shake-Up, and Landing a Role in Ryan Gosling’s ‘Star Wars’ Movie
entry.summary: IndieWire's 'Screen Talk' podcast debates 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth' and welcomes Aaron Pierre for a 'Lanterns' interview.
entry.content:
The topic du jour on this week’s episode of IndieWire’s “Screen Talk” podcast: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.” The movie screened for press ahead of opening on IMAX next week, with divisive reviews for David Fincher’s technician-like take on Quentin Tarantino’s colorfully discursive screenplay that brings back the character of stuntman Cliff Booth (Brad Pitt). Co-hosts Anne Thompson and Ryan Lattanzio debate the film and catch up on the latest developments in the Oscar race — including predictions for the upcoming coastal critics’ awards.

Afterward, Anne is joined by rising British star Aaron Pierre for a chat about HBO’s popular DC series “Lanterns.” When we spoke on Zoom, Pierre had just learned the news of the changes at DC, as his mentors James Gunn and Peter Safran were leaving, replaced by Marvel veteran Jeremy Latchan. He says the right things about how lovely it was to work with them, but he had to be nervous about the fate of his movie still in the editing room, the “Superman” sequel “Man of Tomorrow,” in which he reprises the role of John Stewart, the heir to the Green Lantern throne.

Related Stories
Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a New Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’
Ryan Coogler’s Proximity Media Hires Former Netflix Exec Tendo Nagenda as President

Pierre relates how he landed the role of John Stewart in “Lanterns,” Chris Mundy, Damon Lindelof, and Tom King’s hit HBO series. First, he went through the exploratory “yes, and” audition process. Once he arrived on set, he had to figure out the creative challenge of distinguishing who John Stewart was in the first four episodes from who he was in the last three. The character changes from episode to episode. “The magic was on the page,” said Pierre. “It was our job to bring it to life, bring it into a different place. There were nuances discovered in the moment.”

Pierre also stars in Rachel Morrison’s second feature, “Love of Your Life.” He loved the script and, after he met the director/cinematographer for coffee, decided, “I need to do this role. She has a distinct way of directing. She is enchanted by micro-movements.”

He asked, “Where do I want to be creatively?”

His breakout role was as Michael Cassio on Shakespeare’s Globe stage, with Mark Rylance playing Iago and Andre Holland playing Othello. Before he could step onto the vast stage in front of 1,500 people, he had to conquer his fear. He asked if he could watch Mark Rylance’s rehearsal process and learned that even the greats have to figure it out as they go.

And Pierre explains how he ended up co-starring with Ryan Gosling in Shawn Levy’s “Starfighter,” the latest “Star Wars” movie.

Listen to the episode below or on your preferred podcast platform.

entry.title: Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a New Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’
entry.summary: The filmmaker joins IndieWire's Filmmaker Toolkit podcast to talk about the difficulty of shooting an adventure that takes place in a whale's stomach.
entry.content:
Director Brian Duffield is a cinephile who watches a lot of movies, but when the time came to direct his adventure film “Whalefall” he was dismayed to realize he couldn’t think of a single film he could look to as a model. “It was a nightmare for that reason,” Duffield told IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit podcast. “It also the joy of it, having a room full of amazingly gifted artists all starting from this place of real befuddlement.”

In the movie, Austin Abrams plays a scuba diver who gets swallowed by a sperm whale and has only an hour of oxygen to keep him alive while he tries to escape; it’s a premise that posed multiple challenges for Duffield and his team, starting with the question of how exactly to build the stomach that Abrams would be trapped inside for the majority of the film — and how to shoot those scenes.

Related Stories
Ryan Coogler’s Proximity Media Hires Former Netflix Exec Tendo Nagenda as President
Fall Festival Movies Sold: Magnolia Heaps Dollars on ‘Trash Mountain’ with Caleb Hearon and Zooey Deschanel

“It wasn’t normal coverage,” Duffield said. “Even a shot of Austin just sitting in the stomach required months of preparation and planning — every shot of him in the stomach is, by its nature, a stunt.” The ultimate effect onscreen is terrifying, but on set Duffield says the stomach scenes looked more than a little ridiculous. “The set looked crazy.  From the outside it’s this black weird bag, and then it’s on a gimbal so it’s moving, and it’s full of water.”

To give the impression of the stomach chewing, Duffield’s crew found an old-school, practical solution. “When the stomach chews, it compresses,” Duffield said. “The way we did that is we just had burly men jump onto it. Austin’s inside, and there’s a guy with a camera, and I can’t fit in the stomach so I’m just watching these New Zealanders leap and compress, then I’m hearing Austin scream.” Although Duffield planned his shots meticulously, he often found that the stomach had a mind of its own and required swift adaptation from the crew.

“There’s water in the stomach, and we would drain it every night,” Duffield said. “The material that the stomach was made of would change shape overnight, and we’d come back to resume a scene, and our set would be a different set — we’d fill it with water, and it would all lay different.” Doors also contracted due to humidity and other conditions. “By the end of the shoot, there were so many jagged doors that we’d cut for cameras.”

Ultimately, all of Duffield’s storyboards “went out the window” because the stomach kept changing shape, and Abrams couldn’t roll in the planned directions. “The stomach was kind of directing the movie,” Duffield said. “Austin and I had to sync up and figure out how, with this new environment every day, to get the shots that tell the story as cleanly as possible.” That was no easy task, especially since the set’s very nature made it hard to acclimate the audience geographically.

“It sounds ridiculous, but we had so many conversations about trying to get an audience to see that ‘that sphincter leads to the throat,’ or ‘that sphincter leads to the second stomach,'” Duffield said, adding that he constantly had to think about how one shot would connect to another to let the audience know where Abrams was inside the whale. “Austin’s moving around the whole time, and the stomach goes in every direction. Bit by bit, shot by shot, every shot is its own unique challenge.”

Visual effects supervisor Guillaume Rocheron worked with Duffield and the camera team to come up with visual cues that could help the audience follow Abrams’ journey through the whale, but the task was further complicated by the fact that the audience was sharing his point of view — and for long portions of the story, Abrams’ character was supposed to be confused. “Austin’s character doesn’t have a lot of information about what is happening to him,” Duffield said. “You want the audience to have the same information as him, but not get so lost and confused that they’re out of the movie.”

Duffield knew that striking that balance would be tricky throughout production and editing. “It’s hard to have a character in a situation he doesn’t know anything about and then have an audience get invested,” Duffield said, adding that the usual test screening questions were useless here. “It’s the classic test screening thing: ‘Is there anything that’s confusing to you?'” Luckily, Duffield worked with master editor Pietro Scalia, who worked with the director to find the most straightforward way to connect the audience to the material.

“We eventually concluded, just focus on Austin,” Duffield said. “Austin is dynamite, and he’s carrying you, and the more you’re in lockstep with Austin, you’re going to be okay.” The key, Duffield felt, was to preserve the illusion of reality at every possible moment. “ When we were editing and sound designing, it was just like, ‘How do we keep trying to make it feel real?’ I’m a very pro-CG guy, but even if there’s some stitching from a stuntman or a digital double to Austin, Austin’s in every shot of the scene. I think some of the things that people think is a digital double are not a digital double — it’s Austin just getting yanked around and fighting for his life.”

Though Duffield is sure Abrams wouldn’t want to return for a sequel, he said his lead actor was as up for the physical demands of the role as the department heads were for the mental and logistical challenges — challenges unlike any they had ever faced. “Nothing any of us had done before applied to this project,” Duffield said, adding that nothing they learned would apply to future projects given the singular nature of “Whalefall.” “It was really challenging, but I was looking for that kind of filmmaking challenge. It was the hardest shoot I’ll probably ever have, but everyone was also giddy about it.”

To hear the entire conversation with Brian Duffield and make sure you don’t miss a single episode of Filmmaker Toolkit, subscribe to the podcast on Apple, Spotify, or your favorite podcast platform.

entry.title: Ryan Coogler’s Proximity Media Hires Former Netflix Exec Tendo Nagenda as President
entry.summary: Ryan Coogler's Proximity Media has hired Tendo Nagenda as its new president.
entry.content:
Tendo Nagenda, a former executive on Netflix’s film team, has been tapped as president of Proximity Media, the production company founded by Ryan Coogler, Zinzi Coogler, and Sev Ohanian, the founders announced Thursday.

Nagenda spent four years at Netflix under film chief Scott Stuber, exiting in 2022, and in that time he shepherded films like Spike Lee’s “Da 5 Bloods,” “The Old Guard,” “Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom,” “The Harder They Fall,” and “Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery.”

Nagenda will oversee all aspects of creative development and production at Proximity, including its film, TV, and non-fiction divisions, and will report directly to the founders. The heads of Film, Television and Nonfiction will all report directly to Nagenda, and he’ll work alongside marketing and operations lead Terra Potts and music lead Ludwig Göransson. He starts on November 30.

Related Stories
Fall Festival Movies Sold: Magnolia Heaps Dollars on ‘Trash Mountain’ with Caleb Hearon and Zooey Deschanel
Why the Radical Lesbian Filmmaker Doc ‘Barbara Forever’ Deserves Oscar Recognition

“Tendo has spent his career working alongside talented filmmakers, championing original ideas, and helping make projects that resonate with audiences around the world,” said Ryan Coogler, Zinzi Coogler and Ohanian in a joint statement. “As Proximity continues to grow across film, television, and nonfiction, we’re excited to have his creative instincts and experience helping guide this next chapter. He shares our belief in the power of storytelling to connect people, challenge perspectives and create meaningful impact, and we’re thrilled to welcome him to the team.”

“I’m honored and excited to join Ryan, Zinzi, Sev, and the entire Proximity team,” said Nagenda. “Their commitment to ambitious, meaningful storytelling reflects everything I’ve always believed in, and I look forward to building on what they’ve created, collaborating with extraordinary filmmakers and creators, and bringing compelling new stories to audiences around the world.”

Since leaving Netflix in 2022, Nagenda launched 10 by Ten Entertainment, which produced and released Jeymes Samuel’s “The Book of Clarence” in 2024. Prior to working at Netflix, he had a long track record at Disney and oversaw films on the live-action slate, including “Beauty and the Beast,” “Cinderella,” “Saving Mr. Banks,” “Mulan,” “A Wrinkle in Time,” and “Queen of Katwe.”

Proximity Media had a banner year last year with the release of “Sinners,” which grossed $365 million worldwide. Some of its other features have included “Judas and the Black Messiah,” “Space Jam: A New Legacy,” and “Creed III.” It’s now working on a reboot of “The X-Files” for Hulu starring Danielle Deadwyler and Himesh Patel. Proximity recently entered into a multiyear TV deal with Netflix for scripted and unscripted projects. And it also has produced some nonfiction work including Nat Geo’s hit “Hurricane Katrina: Race Against Time,” as well as other titles like “Stephen Curry: Underrated,” “Homeroom,” and “Anthem.”

Nagenda is a graduate of Claremont McKenna College and a member of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and Producers United. He also serves on the Social Services Committee of the Motion Picture & Television Fund and the board of the UCLA Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center.

entry.title: Why the Radical Lesbian Filmmaker Doc ‘Barbara Forever’ Deserves Oscar Recognition
entry.summary: 'Barbara Forever' director Brydie O'Connor talks her Barbara Hammer documentary, produced by Killer Films.
entry.content:
Finally, a documentary as radical as the lesbian avant-garde feminist filmmaker it’s about. First-time feature filmmaker Brydie O’Connor’s Sundance-winning documentary “Barbara Forever” is a hypnotic archival collage that retraces the life, work, and death of Barbara Hammer.

The documentary, an early fall Strand release produced in partnership with Pamela Koffler and Christine Vachon’s recently Oscar-winning Killer Films, won in Park City for Matt Hixon’s editing. (Kristen Stewart also jumped on board as an executive producer.) It’s not hard to see why. “Barbara Forever” is an archival documentary that unfolds in the shape and style of its subject, an experimental filmmaker who put together some of the first publicly projected lesbian erotica actually made by a lesbian. Voiceover by the filmmaker spans her early career in the Bay Area (and halcyon days as an out lesbian), her 1992 feature debut “Nitrate Kisses,” and the final years of a cancer battle that ended in 2019.

Related Stories
Don’t Forget the Other ‘Heat’ Movie, Which Gave Burt Reynolds One of His Best Noir Roles
Before He Played Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky,’ Star Anthony Ippolito Fought Hard for His Own Big Break

Now New York-based, O’Connor centered her George Washington University thesis project on Hammer’s work before they’d ever met. “I read about Barbara and studied Barbara before I even saw her films,” O’Connor told IndieWire. She reached out to Hammer to “buy her DVDs because they weren’t showing anywhere in D.C. And she wrote back to me. At first, she was a little bit hard on me. She was like, ‘I see you’re writing from an edu.edu address. I just want to make sure that you’re actually a student because if you’re faculty, it would be much, much more expensive.’ [Laughs] And I said, ‘I promise, Barbara, I’m a student. I just can’t wait to see your movies.’ And she sent me her DVDs. So yeah, I think that initial impulse to explore her work was really about … ‘Why don’t more people know about Barbara and her work?'”

Hammer had degrees in psychology and literature before encountering “Meshes of the Afternoon” director Maya Deren’s films (which also influenced David Lynch) at San Francisco State in the 1970s. They lit the fuse for making her own movies. Circa that time, she’d been living in Santa Rosa and married to a man. She came out as a lesbian — busting through that closet, really, with abandon — and took off with her Super 8 camera to start making lesbian films. Growing up in Kansas, O’Connor, in her early 30s, resonated with Hammer’s early biography, and Hammer’s early lust for self-reinvention.

“She was not really tentative about anything. She picked up a camera in her late 20s as she was getting a divorce from a man when she realized that she was a lesbian and she made her film,” O’Connor said. “She learned by doing. And I was so inspired because, at the time, I was studying American studies and history in school. I had no background in the arts really, except for enjoying consuming them. And I really thought I would be a film critic or a writer… [Barbara Hammer] was not afraid to fail creatively. And she tried so many different ideas, of course, throughout her entire career in making over 85 films, but especially in that first decade of her career.”

Post-college and in New York, O’Connor, who’s spent “a decade in the Hammer world, and my entire adult consciousness,” would see Hammer at the Metrograph in Lower Manhattan. “I definitely was ‘the girl who wrote her thesis on Barbara,’ probably one of many, and I was day-playing in the film industry,” O’Connor said. “I would occasionally go up to Yale, where her formal archive is held, to continue doing independent research. I was looking at her love letters and her photographs… I wrote to her in January of 2019 when I was about to make my first short film. I said, ‘Hi, Barbara.’ I didn’t know how sick she was at the time. I was like, ‘I’m making my first film. Can I take you to coffee? Do you have any advice for me?’ And she wrote back to me and said, ‘I’m at the very, very end of my life, but best of luck with everything in your career.'”

Hammer died in March 2019, which is when O’Connor contacted the filmmaker’s partner, the human rights advocate Florrie Burke. “Florrie was the love of her life. They were together for 31 years,” O’Connor said. Their meeting culminated in O’Connor’s 2022 short film “Love, Barbara,” which she expanded into the feature that hit theaters this year. In a 2026 Oscar documentary race heavy on genocide and social issues — or a three-hour A24 movie that’s shaken up the entire form — “Barbara Forever” is life-affirming, lovely, yet still-important counter-programming.

The organic archival rhythm of “Barbara Forever” eschews talking heads altogether, instead conversing with what Hammer’s work looked and felt like. One of the film’s most charming snippets finds Hammer showing one of her (SFW!) films to a classroom of small schoolchildren. They end up having an unexpected appreciation for the experimental film clip’s non-narrative sensibilities.

O’Connor collaborated with Burke on sifting through 35 hours of audio recordings to stitch together a narration unfolding entirely in Hammer’s own words. “Florrie was so happy with [the short], but she always reminded me there’s so much more to Barbara than just our relationship,” O’Connor said. “Barbara’s this huge personality. She’s so charismatic and charming and really both thoughtful, but also very savvy. She wanted to be recognized. She wanted to be known for her work and her efforts, and she was uncompromising in what she made and how she shared her work. So it just made sense that she would be the narrator of the film.”

The Sundance-winning editing, too, proved a challenge, as O’Connor and her filmmaking team pored over more than 400 hours of visual material — from Hammer’s films, to outtakes, B-sides, home videos, and more. “I really wanted to convey with this film: Why did Barbara turn the camera on herself and her life and her lovers and her body as a method of alternative history making? What did she see in the value of that approach and then making experimental cinema out of it and demanding the value of that within culture?”

That Hammer’s work wasn’t more canonized during her life — an effort O’Connor has made partly her own, especially as a new digital restoration of “Nitrate Kisses” is making the rounds — isn’t only because of how confrontational she was about gender and her own sexuality. “Nitrate Kisses” is, after all, an experimental movie about lesbian repression dating back to the early 20th century. Is it also that autofiction and individualism, now a dominant mode of contemporary artistic expression, were also marginalized at that point within her particular corner of the art world?

“She was both an experimental filmmaker and avant-garde artist and a lesbian filmmaker. And she says, and this was something she said all throughout her life and career, that she didn’t fit neatly into either category where she could just build an audience within that space,” O’Connor said. “She really was uncompromising about being both and working at the intersection of both and having both audiences… The experimental film world didn’t necessarily want to see lesbian work, didn’t necessarily want to see the nude woman’s body on screen. And lesbians, there was not so much representation, especially in the ’70s, ’80s, ’90s, increasingly so, but her work was experimental and thought-provoking, and she felt like a lot of her queer audiences wanted more realistic depictions of queerness.”

O’Connor, who received a 2026 Creative Capital to not only finish her work on “Barbara Forever” but also continue making docs, said, “The industry is hard, but that certainly won’t stop me from making nonfiction films. I’m just excited to pivot to my next project.”

“Barbara Forever” is now available to stream on PVOD platforms.

entry.title: Don’t Forget the Other ‘Heat’ Movie, Which Gave Burt Reynolds One of His Best Noir Roles
entry.summary: 40 years ago, Reynolds starred in this crime drama from screenwriter William Goldman that remains an underrated and underseen example of 'Burt Noir.'
entry.content:
40 years ago, the crime drama “Heat” opened in France and received positive reviews from Paris critics. No, not the “Heat” directed by Michael Mann that starred Robert De Niro and Al Pacino and would go on to become a revered classic — that came nine years later. The “Heat” that played in Europe in 1986 starred Burt Reynolds, was directed by multiple journeyman helmers, and was almost immediately forgotten only months after it limped into U.S. theaters in March of 1987.

American reviewers dismissed “Heat” with casual cruelty, but as so often happens in film history — think Jerry Lewis, Michael Cimino’s “Heaven’s Gate,” or Brian De Palma’s “Mission to Mars” — the French got our cinema right where our own critics got it embarrassingly wrong. “Heat,” in which Reynolds plays an aging mercenary held prisoner by a crippling gambling addiction, is not only one of Reynolds’ most interesting films but one of his most personal, and a top-tier entry in the canon of the subgenre that is “Burt Noir.”

Related Stories
Before He Played Sylvester Stallone in ‘I Play Rocky,’ Star Anthony Ippolito Fought Hard for His Own Big Break
‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: David Fincher’s Breezy Tarantino Spinoff Is a Disappointing Compromise Between Great Directors

From early on, one of the most interesting things about Burt Reynolds was the tension between his affable onscreen persona — the smiling, charming fellow who had major box office hits with crowd-pleasers like “Smokey and the Bandit” and “The Cannonball Run” — and the visible agitation simmering underneath. Reynolds was one of the premier talk show guests (and occasional guest hosts) of the 1970s and early 1980s, a guy who could always be counted on to tell a funny, self-deprecating anecdote that made the audience feel like a part of his inner circle.

But Reynolds always gave the sense that there was a chip on his shoulder — that he was mad about not being taken seriously enough, or being taken too seriously, or losing out on the best parts to his friend and competitor Clint Eastwood and other stars. (Never mind the fact that Reynolds lost out on most of his potentially successful roles — “Terms of Endearment,” “Die Hard,” “Pretty Woman” — because he turned them down, not because anyone took them from him.)

Early on, Eastwood let his controlled rage be a defining trait of his star persona; Reynolds generally tried, and failed, to cloak his under chuckling humility. Many of Reynolds’ best performances exploit this tension, from John Boorman’s “Deliverance,” in which Reynolds’ male bonding fishing expedition descends into a horror, to Paul Thomas Anderson’s “Boogie Nights,” in which the actor’s initially nurturing father figure turns dark and violent when tested.

Reynolds’ memoir, “But Enough About Me,” offers a fascinating glimpse into the contradiction between his healthy self-regard (hilariously exhibited in passages in which he disparages two of the best directors he ever worked with, Anderson and Peter Bogdanovich) and his persistent self-loathing (demonstrated in his candid appraisals of his many terrible personal and professional decisions). The latter informs an ongoing, if intermittent, cycle of Reynolds movies of which “Heat” is a key example: movies I define as “Burt Noir,” in which the actor plays supremely confident men of action tormented by regret and the knowledge that they’ve failed to live up to their potential.

The first, and possibly best, example of Burt Noir is the 1975 cop drama “Hustle,” in which Reynolds plays a Los Angeles detective surrounded by moral decay and corruption. Reynolds and director Robert Aldrich got to make “Hustle” after their commercial success with “The Longest Yard,” and they immediately squandered whatever mainstream goodwill that comedy had bought them with a film so grim and pessimistic it made James Ellroy look like Fred Rogers.

In “Hustle,” Reynolds is surrounded by evil both banal and terrifying, and he meets almost all of it with a weary resignation — aside from one desperate, possibly pointless act, he doesn’t even try to fight the men to whom he knows he is morally, intellectually, and physically superior. The movie reeks with sadness in spite of being marketed as a muscular action movie — though it is a muscular action movie, as is a later and more commercially successful Burt Noir, “Sharky’s Machine.” 

That movie, in which Reynolds plays a cop who falls for the prostitute he’s got under surveillance, further explores the sense of moral outrage that marked “Hustle” and Reynolds’ directorial debut, “Gator,” and it gives Reynolds another of his tortured heroes who alternates between spurts of violent action and long passages of almost complete impotence — a combination that reaches its apotheosis in “Heat.”

A clue to what Reynolds is up to in terms of deconstructing his persona comes in the opening of “Heat,” a 12-minute prologue that doesn’t have much to do with the rest of the film other than breaking down Reynolds’ heroic image for audience members who still see him as a conventional leading man. Reynolds’ Nick Escalante tries to pick up a woman in a bar in the ugliest, aggressive way possible, and it’s confusing for the audience — why has the guy who was such a sweet charmer to Sally Field, Goldie Hawn, Jill Clayburgh, and Julie Andrews in earlier movies turned into such a misogynistic pig?

Even more confusing is what follows, when the meek twerp the woman is dating shows up and beats the hell out of Reynolds in the parking lot. We learn, later on, that the whole thing was a set-up — the guy hired Nick to fake everything so he could look like a hero in front of his girlfriend. But in the audience’s mind, the seed has already been planted; subconsciously we can never quite see this guy as a straightforward hero, and that’s the way Reynolds and screenwriter William Goldman want it.

The film progresses as a kind of hangout movie familiar to anyone who loves Quentin Tarantino’s “Jackie Brown” or “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth”; there’s a relatively solid genre movie structure running underneath everything, but Goldman takes plenty of time for character-developing digressions that give the whole movie a rich sense of melancholy texture.

Escalante’s tale of attempted moral redemption in the form of his efforts to help the victim of a sadistic young gangster avenge her beating moves from sharp wit (in the form of the best dialogue Goldman ever wrote — which is saying something when you’re talking about the guy who wrote “Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid”) and contemplative scenes of self-examination to shocking bursts of expertly choreographed violence and wistful romance.

It’s all given added layers of irony and resonance by the Las Vegas setting, which seems to mock Escalante’s dreams of hitting it big and escaping to a peaceful retirement in Italy, and Goldman’s choice to set the movie at Christmas, which only mocks Escalante more cruelly. Although “Heat” is one of Goldman’s least well known films (a movie that is easily forgotten amidst the more honored “All the President’s Men,” “Marathon Man,” and “Misery”), it’s one of his most beautifully written, with badinage as snappy as it is revealing and a weaving plot whose emotional effects really sneak up on you.

So why were American critics so dismissive? As is so often the case, they mostly seemed to be reviewing the chaotic circumstances of the production more than the movie that actually resulted from them. “Heat” was a famously troubled movie, whose misfortunes made their way into the press long before the film actually hit American screens. Its beginnings were auspicious: Goldman, one of the most respected writers in the business, was adapting his own novel (with a clause in his contract that said he couldn’t be rewritten), and Robert Altman was set to direct.

Then, only days before shooting, Altman quit the project after his favored cinematographer, Canadian cameraman Pierre Mignot, was denied an H-1 Visa to work in America. Altman claimed that over the course of eight pictures he had developed a style and way of working with Mignot that he didn’t want to abandon, and certainly didn’t want to have to reinvent in a matter of days with another director of photography. Whether or not this is the whole story is anybody’s guess — it was reported that the real reason Altman left had to do with creative differences between him and producer Elliott Kastner, and that Mignot merely gave him the excuse he was looking for to walk.

Goldman suggested Reynolds, who had helmed “Sharky’s Machine” and other fine pictures, take over directing himself, but Burt said he wanted to focus solely on his performance. Thus began a game of directorial musical chairs that would be widely reported and which gave “Heat” the patina of a disaster in the making. Reliable craftsman Dick Richards came on first, only to leave the production after getting into a fistfight with Reynolds on the set. In spite of lawsuits flying back and forth, Richards returned to the set, only to leave again when he fell off a camera crane and ended up in the hospital.

On the days when Richards was out second-unit director and stunt coordinator Stan Barrett took on directing duties, and some of the most electrifying moments in “Heat” can be attributed to him. Barrett had worked as Reynolds’ stunt double for more than 20 years and had a great sense of how to capitalize on the actor’s physicality and image, and the set pieces he directed for “Heat” — like a hotel room fight between Reynolds and some thugs — are beautifully staged and filled with brutally effective and original instances of sudden and shocking violence.

DGA rules at the time prohibited Barrett from taking over the reins for more than five days, since the guild forbade any preexisting member of a troupe from replacing the director — a rule, ironically, that was created when Reynolds’ friend Clint Eastwood fired director Philip Kaufman from “The Outlaw Josey Wales” and replaced him with himself. With only eight days of filming left on “Heat,” television stalwart Jerry Jameson (who had directed Reynolds years earlier on “Dan August”) stepped in and finished the picture.

The experience doesn’t seem to have been a happy one for many of the principals involved, especially Richards, who gave interviews begging people not to blame him for what he saw as the film’s failures. A DGA arbitration determined that Richards was responsible for 40% of the film — more than any of the other directors on the project — and thus should have the credit. Not wanting his name on the movie, Richards eschewed his usual credit for “Directed by R.M. Richards” and tried to wash his hands of the entire debacle as soon as he could.

With the movie’s own director badmouthing the film in the press, “Heat” never really stood a chance. Yet the movie that exists doesn’t show signs of any of the production’s dysfunction, aside from a slightly abrupt and abbreviated finale (one of several that was shot). In the end, Goldman and Reynolds, more than any director, are the true auteurs of “Heat,” and the consistency of their conception of Nick Escalante as an honorable, self-destructive, romantic, tortured, possibly doomed hero gives “Heat” a lingering emotional resonance and power that still works 40 years later.

Burt would continue his forays into Burt Noir both in film (“Malone,” “Rent-A-Cop,” “Physical Evidence”) and television (“B.L. Stryker,” “Hard Time”), but he never played this kind of character better than he did in “Heat.” The movie was remade, incidentally, in 2015 by “Con Air” director Simon West as “Wild Card.” That version didn’t connect with critics or audiences either, in spite of Goldman once again writing the screenplay. At this point it’s fair to assume that “Heat” is just a doomed project, which is a shame — since it also happens to represent one of Goldman’s finest artistic moments.

entry.title: ‘The Gilded Age’ Renewed for Fifth Season Following Ratings Boom
entry.summary: 'The Gilded Age' renewed for fifth season following a surge in ratings.
entry.content:
Fans of “The Gilded Age,” rejoice! There are still more luncheons to plan, more balls to savor, and more opera opening nights to fight over. Yes, the HBO original series has been renewed for a fifth season.

The move follows a surge in popularity that began with the show’s drama-filled third season, which saw Bertha (Carrie Coon) and George Russell’s (Morgan Spector) relationship strain, and has continued with the fourth season, which has dealt with their marriage troubles, the wedding of Peggy Scott (Denée Benton), and a visit from Grover Cleveland.

Clearly, it’s working. Viewership for Season 4 has grown week over week, HBO stated in a press release. Episode 3 hit a season high of 4.3 million U.S. cross-platform viewers and episodes are averaging 5.9 million viewers and growing. That outpaces the prior season by nearly 20 percent.

Related Stories
‘Dig’ Review: Amy Poehler’s Talent-Rich Peacock Comedy Barely Scratches the Surface
‘The Altruists’ Review: Netflix’s Slight Sam Bankman-Fried Series Tells a Strange, Crooked Love Story

The turnaround is striking because “The Gilded Age” was very much on the bubble for most of its first two seasons. Bringing 19th-century high-society to life is expensive, and the show initially struggled to become a ratings powerhouse despite being co-created by Julian Fellowes of “Downton Abbey” fame. In interviews, the cast admitted that they often feared they would be canceled. But audiences have shown up in a big way, and Fellowes and his co-creator Sonja Warfield recently told IndieWire that they have more stories to tell beyond this season.

“We have a Season 5 in us if we’re allowed to do it,” Fellowes said. “But when you write a TV series, you have to finish every season so that it could be the end, because one day it will be.”

In its three eligible seasons, “The Gilded Age” has earned 15 total Emmy nominations, including Outstanding Drama Series and Outstanding Directing for a Drama Series, as well as a Screen Actors Guild Award nomination for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series.

“The Gilded Age” cast includes Christine Baranski, Cynthia Nixon, Louisa Jacobson, Taissa Farmiga, Harry Richardson, Blake Ritson, Ben Ahlers, Ashlie Atkinson, Dylan Baker, Kelley Curran, Jordan Donica, Jessica Frances Dukes, Amy Forsyth, Jack Gilpin, Simon Jones, Celia Keenan-Bolger, Ben Lamb, Audra McDonald, Brian Stokes Mitchell, Debra Monk, Hattie Morahan, Donna Murphy, and Kristine Nielsen.

“The Gilded Age” is a co-production between HBO and Universal Television, a division of Universal Studio Group.

entry.title: ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: David Fincher’s Breezy Tarantino Spinoff Is a Disappointing Compromise Between Great Directors
entry.summary: Hollywood's chillest stuntman returns in David Fincher's 'Once Upon a Time in Hollywood' follow-up, 'The Further Mis-adventures of Cliff Booth.'
entry.content:
The scratchy “vintage” Netflix logo says everything so well that the rest of the movie almost feels like it’s belaboring the point: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is a story about a town where half the people are dreaming up the future, the other half are desperate to mythologize the past, and all of them are stuck together in the ugly compromise we call the right fucking now.

Then again, “story” might be too strong a word for the unbothered zen noir that Quentin Tarantino has spun off from his 1969-set hit “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” which memorably ended with former TV Western star Rick Dalton and his longtime stuntman Cliff Booth saving Manson Family victim Sharon Tate from the cruel fate that befell her in real life. Los Angeles was built on the promise that history could be rewritten, and that anyone who made their way onto a studio lot could print the legend, but the present is another beast altogether. It’s feral. Unforgiving. It has to be survived before it can be shaped into a story worth telling, even if that isn’t much of a story at all.

Related Stories
Film Independent’s New President Wants to Build an L.A. Powerhouse — and Shake Up the Spirit Awards
‘Dig’ Review: Amy Poehler’s Talent-Rich Peacock Comedy Barely Scratches the Surface

After decades of trafficking in ultra-fetishistic nostalgia (and continued years of refusing to close the book on his own legend), Tarantino has scripted a conditional surrender to the forward march of time — a film whose modest and spectacularly unbothered protagonist invites his egomaniacal and constantly agitated creator to make a certain peace with the inevitable fact of being left behind. And though it was initially Tarantino’s plan to direct that film himself, handing the reins of this breezy showbiz throwback to modern Hollywood’s most unsentimental technician forces “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” into a muted but fascinating tug-of-war between the past tense and the future perfect (even if that scratchy “vintage” Netflix logo articulates the same tension with a greater clarity of purpose than any other part of this perverse collaboration).

Pleasant enough for a movie so dark, and strangely relaxed for a movie so deeply self-conflicted, “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is ultimately a story — there’s that word again — about someone changing with the times without letting the times change them in return. It takes place over the span of a few days in the summer of 1977 (even though it builds to the October premiere of “Looking for Mr. Goodbar,” which I suppose might have happened a few months earlier in this parallel universe), when “Star Wars” is the biggest force on Earth and the tough guys of yore are being phased out by the very different kind of daring that New Hollywood brought to the table. Once upon a time, Cliff Booth did his business supporting Rick Dalton on the big screen — reborn here as the lead of a David Fincher film, he’s reintroduced working the projector at the New Beverly Cinema like the hyper-chill uncle Tyler Durden never had (digital cigarette burns and all).

If “The Further Mis-Adventures” doesn’t belabor the reel change from one generation of movies to another, that’s because Cliff doesn’t either. He’s just happy to be there — still hot, cool, and at total peace with himself despite an increasingly violent reputation (a state of mind Brad Pitt might relate to). The world around him is a lot uglier than it was eight years ago, as the vibrant celluloid memory palace of Tarantino’s film has faded into the computational muddiness that Fincher has come to mistake for the truth, but that “don’t mean shit” to Cliff.

Drab cinematography and bad disco aren’t enough to unsettle a guy who lied about his age so that he could join the Philippine resistance as a teenager during World War II. A guy who spontaneously killed his own wife in the span of a shrugged-off flashback, and beat up Bruce Lee as part of a controversial backstory that Tarantino can’t quite bring himself to disavow. Besides, Cliff doesn’t want for glory — he delights in sharing a small apartment with his TV-obsessed dad in Marina del Rey (Gus Booth is played by a winsome and wonderful Peter Weller), and always demurs when someone insists that they know him from somewhere, which is all the time. Manning the booth at a half-empty Fairfax grindhouse might seem like a fall from grace, but — as “Anora” favorite Karren Karagulian learns the hard way in the movie’s self-contained opening scene — underestimate Cliff Booth at your own peril.

Of course, that isn’t Cliff’s only job. If anything, the gig at the New Bev is just a convenient front for his far more lucrative work as a Hollywood fixer, which sees him apply his curious but unyielding moral code to a wide variety of situations — even if Fincher’s movie only has the bandwidth to illustrate a small handful of them. Tarantino might be drawn to the discursive plotting of an Elmore Leonard paperback, but after watching any number of Netflix TV shows that should have been shortened into movies, it’s a cruel irony to see two of our greatest filmmakers slush their talents together into a movie that should have serialized into a long-running TV show, complete with a new guest star every week.

Alas, that’s not the world that streaming hath wrought, and so we have to settle for shape-shifting content that seems equally ill-suited to both small and big screens alike, the elasticity of its intended presentation reflected by the ambiguity of a plot that drifts from a casual hangout session to a brutal crime-thriller and a sweetly abrasive romance without ever becoming much of anything. These different energies ultimately collect around a manic and lunkheaded TV actor named Charlie Peters (a very game Scott Caan, channeling his father), who’s compensated for being short by doing all of his own stunts.

Ordinarily that would give him little reason to link up with Cliff Booth, but it turns out that old Charlie got a little too drunk in Manila one night and put a hit out on his wife, Toni (Carla Gugino), who once made her own sad bid for stardom. After sobering up and falling back in love with his bride, Charlie hoped to call the whole thing off, but the two psychotic Filipino hitmen who just landed in L.A. (Matt Groove and JB Tadena as ruthless brothers Mr. Verdusco and Mr. Verdusco) refuse to go home without being made whole, and so it’s up to Cliff to make everyone happy.

Sounds easy enough, but then we get to the most crucial part: Cliff Booth has a crush. A big one. Or maybe tall would be a better choice of words. Her name is Karen Crosby, she’s Charlie’s exasperated agent, and she’s played by a luminous Elizabeth Debicki (sporting her native Australian accent), who’s charmed by Cliff’s modesty and the slight embarrassment of his machismo. He knows exactly who he is in a town where everyone is busy pretending to be somewhere else, and the drawling magic of Pitt’s performance — which he continues to wear like a second skin — is that he always seems to be content with living in the moment at hand. It’s all a big goof, which is exactly why he’ll kill you for getting in the way of a good story.

Karen, on the other hand, is a former critic who resents Hollywood for the same reason that Cliff is so at home there, and their mutual ability to see each other through the spectacle of it all is a perfect template for how Tarantino and Fincher might have found some common ground. Tarantino gets off on memorializing a world gone by (brace for long conversations about Ralph Meeker’s body fat, along with an extended deep-dive into the nuances of network TV in the ’60s), while Fincher tolerates it as an excuse to play with the tech required to make it look like Johnny Carson is talking to Charlie Peters.

Although slapdash and forgettable by Tarantino’s standards, the writing naturally wants to swim in this strange trench of Tinseltown history. The direction, by contrast, seems motivated by finding the most efficient path to shore. Fincher lives for the thrill of solving things only he would see as problems in the first place, and that mindset proves as contradictory to Cliff Booth’s laid-back, leathery ethos as it is perfectly aligned with the Swiss-watch precision of the hitman in “The Killer.”

Tarantino sees this as a séance, Fincher as a math equation, and while the tension between those approaches can be rich in theme, it’s often dull in function. Neither of these name-brand auteurs is willing to let go as much as the movie they’re making together insists they should, so “The Further Mis-Adventures” ultimately dilutes them both instead of sparking some kind of unexpected kismet between them. It’s no wonder that the scenes between Cliff and Karen accomplish exactly that, as each of them surrenders to the lack of control they share with each other. (A dynamic illustrated through the chaos of an Infinity Racing sequence that ends with the movie’s driest visual joke, a too-rare instance of Cliff making good on his insistence that he’s “a little funny.”)

The film is too watchable for that to sting as much as it could, but the small handful of electric scenes where those dueling energies feel complementary — the climactic sitdown between Cliff and the Verdusco brothers comes to mind — are forced to carry the weight of so much wasted potential. Don’t give me Yahya Abdul-Mateen II as a football-player-turned-Blaxploitation-star if you’re just going to kneecap him like that! Don’t let Karen deride American movies as “hamburgers” if you’re going to make us settle for steak tartare.

Of course, “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” had a similar hard-on for delayed gratification, and for evoking a world that it didn’t have time to more fully explore before it disappeared forever. But that movie was living on borrowed time, this one is striving to live outside of time altogether. “In Hollywood,” Gus says, “two things matter: shelf life, and shelf space.” Neither of those things matter to Cliff Booth — or to the company distributing his mis-adventures. He just wants to make the best of the moment at hand. It can be a lot of fun to watch him try, but it still feels like he’s forced to settle for the present in the end.

Grade: B-

Netflix will release “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” in IMAX theaters on Wednesday, November 25. It will be available to stream on Netflix starting Wednesday, December 23.

entry.title: Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Woman Unknown,’ May el-Toukhy’s Golden Lion Winner, Sells to Cohen Media Group
entry.summary: Movies like 'Babies,' 'Ink,' and 'Elsinore' have already sold to distributors ahead of their world premieres at TIFF, Venice, and Telluride.
entry.content:
What will the buyers be snapping up at the fall festivals? With this year’s Toronto International Film Festival already touting a high number of premieres for movies that originally bowed at Cannes or Sundance, there’s fewer world premiere sales titles that aren’t already with distributors than we’re used to. Still, the festival (with its very first market in place), plus Telluride, Venice, and New York are loaded with options, and there’s always the potential for another historic breakout like last year’s “Obsession.”

We’ll be tracking all the sales as they come in here, so check back frequently.

Films Acquired After the Festivals

“Woman Unknown”

Distributor: Cohen Media Group
Director: May el-Toukhy
Festival: Venice Competition
Buzz: Venice’s top prize winner of the Golden Lion has found a U.S. deal, this one made out of AFM with Cohen Media Group. Not only did el-Toukhy (“Queen of Hearts,” “The Crown”) movie win the Golden Lion this year, star Mathilde Arcel also won the Volpi Cup for Best Actress. The Danish film, also Denmark’s official Oscar selection, is a period drama set after World War II about a former housekeeper now set to be married to the household’s wealthy patriarch. But as she plans an extravagant dinner party to celebrate the occasion, hidden aspects of her past begin to resurface. Namely, it has to do with Danish witch hunts of those associated with Nazis after the war, and our positive review called it an “angry, despairing film” with a “Haneke-level bleakness in its assessment of human nature.” Cohen Media Group also recently bought an Isabelle Huppert comedy called “All About Corinne” that played at TIFF and premiered at Locarno.

Related Stories
‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations
What Makes a Good Oscar Campaign? Just Ask Sony Classics’ Michael Barker and Tom Bernard

“The Julia Set”

Distributor: Sony Pictures Classics
Director: Niki Byrne
Festival: TIFF Special Presentations
Buzz: Sony Pictures Classics have acquired all rights in the United States, Benelux, Switzerland, Italy, Scandinavia, Spain, United Kingdom, Eastern Europe (excluding Poland), Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Israel and Asia (excluding Singapore) to “The Julia Set,” written and directed by Niki Byrne. The film had its world premiere at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival and follows a gifted young math prodigy (“One Battle After Another” breakout Chase Infiniti) who is “recruited into an elite prep course culminating in the most punishing exam in mathematics, while at the same time falling into a romantic relationship with her charismatic teaching assistant, Pascal (Christopher Briney).”

“The Daughters of Abraham”

Distributor: Strand Releasing
Director: Hanaël El Yousfi
Festival: TIFF Discovery
Buzz: This directorial debut follows two friends, one Muslim and one Jewish, spending a carefree summer in Marseille, only to see the expectations and tensions between their traditional families start to get in the way of their friendship and leads them to take hold of their own destinies. El Yousfi both wrote and directed the feature, co-writing it with Raphaël Chevènement and Mia Grace Brown. It had its international premiere at TIFF, but it actually had a small bow at a French festival called the Angoulême Francophone Film Festival, where it won an Audience Award and a Special Prize for its cast. “The Daughters of Abraham” first opens in France on December 30. But Strand, a Culver City-based distributor behind recent releases like Mexico’s Oscar submission “On the Road,” “In a Whisper,” and the 4K restoration of Gregg Araki’s “Mysterious Skin,” will release it in North America in 2027.

“Honeymoon/Funeral”

Distributor: Black Bear
Director: Nahnatchka Khan
Festival: TIFF Market
Buzz: This market title is a rom-com starring an indelible trio of Greta Lee, Rebecca Ferguson, and Carrie Coon, and it wrapped production in September. Read more about the film here.

Films Acquired During the Festivals

“A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra”

Distributor: 1-2 Special
Director: Jacqueline Lentzou
Festival: Venice Orizzonti
Buzz: This Greek coming-of-age story won filmmaker Jacqueline Lentzou the Best Director prize in the Horizons section of the Venice Film Festival, but 1-2 Special picked it up after its North American premiere at NYFF and head of additional screenings at BFI London Film Festival, the Chicago International Film Festival, and the Busan International Film Festival. Blending what the release describes as both the “cosmic and the mundane,” the film follows a 15-year-old girl who meets a new classmate named Phaedra but also begins to notice signs and symbols from a dream world surfacing around her, ultimately leading her to an ethereal transformation. This is Lentzou’s second feature after 2021’s “Moon, 66 Questions.” 1-2 Special is planning a theatrical release for 2027.

“The Surgeon”

Distributor: Sony Pictures
Director: Roshan Sethi
Festival: TIFF Centrepiece
Buzz: This action-thriller starring Michelle Yeoh as a surgeon who is abducted and forced to operate on a mysterious patient is a bit of a departure for Sethi. Sethi’s previous film was the charming rom-com “A Nice Indian Boy,” and he’s also the co-creator of the medical drama “The Resident.” But reviews for the film were solid, and it’s not typical for the majors to buy festival titles, but Sony is already dating it for release on April 2, 2027.

“River”

Distributor: Universal Pictures and Blumhouse Atomic Monster
Director: Joshua Giuliano
Festival: TIFF Midnight Madness
Buzz: IndieWire first broke the news about the film originally set up at the Independent Film Company and Shudder being picked up by Universal and Blumhouse Atomic Monster for a deal that could surpass $10 million as the companies hope to find the next “Obsession,” just as they did last year. Read more here.

“Rapinoe”

Distributor: HBO Documentary Films
Director: Rebecca Huntt
Festival: TIFF Docs
Buzz: “Rapinoe” about US Women’s National Soccer star Megan Rapinoe was the opening night documentary at TIFF. Rapinoe was in attendance at the premiere screening of director Rebecca Huntt’s (“Beba”) film, which grapples more with Rapinoe’s progressive politics, such as her kneeling in solidarity with Colin Kaepernick, and her coming out story, than it does on the stories from her soccer career about how she led the US Women’s team to two World Cup titles, an Olympics Gold, and the Ballon d’Or. HBO Documentary Films has North American TV and streaming rights to the film. THR first reported the news.

Films Acquired Before the Festivals

“Babies”

Distributor: Roadside Attractions and Vertical
Director: Lauren Miller Rogen
Festival: TIFF Gala Presentation
Buzz: Lauren Miller Rogen directs her husband Seth Rogen alongside Anna Kendrick and Kate Berlant in this comedy about parenthood and prospective parenthood. It follows a childless couple who begin debating the merits of having kids when their divorced friend and her child move in with them. The cast is stacked, including Issa Rae, Dan Stevens, Zach Cherry, Ed Helms, Ashley Park, Sharon Stone, and David Strathairn in supporting parts.

“Babies” is described as heartfelt and poignant in what is shaping up to be a strong year for Seth Rogen. The movie launched sales at TIFF nearly a year to the date prior to its Roy Thomson Hall premiere. The distributors are planning for a release in early 2027.

“Elsinore”

Distributor: Focus Features
Director: Simon Stone
Festival: Telluride and TIFF
Buzz: Andrew Scott is said to be fantastic in this performance based on the true story of “Chariots of Fire” and “Gandhi” star and thespian Ian Charleson, who died of AIDS at the age of 40 but managed to raise awareness for the epidemic after his death. Focus has already dated the film for late November, the same time slot it gave “Hamnet” last year.

“Ink”

Distributor: Netflix
Director: Danny Boyle
Festival: Venice Competition
Buzz: The opening night film for this year’s Biennale, “Ink” is the story of the birth of The Sun tabloid in the ’60s and the collaboration between editor Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) and Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) that made it the notorious publication it is today. Netflix didn’t acquire worldwide rights to the film, so it could easily be something it sees as both commercial and an awards play.
